legend: Ariel is on a vacation where he must visit n$$$n$$$ locations famous for their cereal, numbered 1…n$$$1 \dots n$$$.
He will visit all the locations in some order, where the i$$$i$$$th location he visits is ai$$$a_i$$$.

Therefore, his order of visiting locations forms a permutation of length n$$$n$$$. Note that a permutation of length n$$$n$$$ is a sequence containing every number from 1…n$$$1 \dots n$$$ exactly once.

Ariel thinks an amazing permutation is one where there are no indices (i,j,k)$$$(i, j, k)$$$ where (1≤i<j<k≤n$$$1 \le i  \lt  j  \lt  k \leq n$$$) such that j−i=k−j$$$j - i = k - j$$$ and aj−ai=ak−aj$$$a_j - a_i = a_k - a_j$$$.
Find a permutation of 1…n$$$1 \dots n$$$ that satisfies this (the i$$$i$$$th number is the i$$$i$$$th location Ariel visits).
output: A single line containing a space separated permutation of 1…n$$$1 \dots n$$$ such that Ariel has an amazing vacation.
Any output satisfying the above constraints will be accepted.
note: If we take the first sample case output, no three indices validate the above condition.

Another example would be (i,j,k)$$$(i, j, k)$$$ = (1,2,3)$$$(1, 2, 3)$$$. Although, j−i=k−j$$$j - i = k - j$$$ since 2−1=3−2$$$2 - 1 = 3 - 2$$$, aj−ai≠ak−aj$$$a_j - a_i \neq a_k - a_j$$$ since 4−2≠2−1$$$4 - 2 \neq 2 - 1$$$.
